claims.statement: The dashboard backend is a single FastAPI APIRouter created in agent/dashboard/routes.py with prefix "/dashboard/api", and it is mounted onto the composed FastAPI app in agent/api/app.py via app.include_router(dashboard_router).

agent/dashboard/__init__.py exposes the router lazily via a PEP 562 __getattr__ so that importing a dashboard submodule does not drag in routes.py, FastAPI, and every API/job module; only the webapp that mounts the router pays that import cost.

GitHub login issues a signed state carrying a hashed nonce stored in a short-lived state cookie and redirects to GitHub's authorize URL; the callback validates the state nonce against the cookie, exchanges the code, enforces an organization login gate, persists the token, and issues a signed session JWT in the session cookie.

Session cookie Secure/SameSite flags are derived from the API scheme: an HTTPS DASHBOARD_API_BASE_URL yields Secure; SameSite=None (cross-site production), otherwise local http falls back to SameSite=Lax without Secure.

Every mutating dashboard request is guarded by the router-level dependency require_same_origin_for_mutations, which passes GET/HEAD/OPTIONS and bearer-token-only requests but rejects cookie-authenticated mutations whose Origin/Referer is not in the dashboard allowlist with a CSRF error.

require_session decodes the session cookie or raises 401, and admin-only endpoints additionally check is_admin while some CI endpoints accept an Actions OIDC token or an admin GitHub PAT instead of a session cookie.
The thread detail endpoint returns metadata only and does no server-side message conversion because the client SDK hydrates the transcript itself by reading GET .../state.

The cloud terminal is exposed as POST /threads/{id}/terminal/connect (returning a WebSocket URL, subprotocol, and short-lived signed ticket) plus a WS /threads/{id}/terminal endpoint that requires a LangSmith sandbox, is capacity-bounded by a semaphore, and bridges the browser to a PTY shell in the thread's sandbox.

The ui/ app is a TanStack Start file-based-route app whose key routes include agents (with nested threads, local, environments, instructions, sandbox), review and $owner.$repo.pull.$number, admin and admin_.evals, usage, cloud-agents, my-settings, and login.
The ui/ integrations route is a redirect to my-settings because integrations were folded into Profile Settings.
The browser calls /dashboard/api/* as a same-origin relative path so the session cookie is sent, and the UI server proxies those calls to the Python backend rather than sending them cross-origin.

In deployed builds ui/server/backend-proxy.ts is a Nitro handler for /dashboard/api/** and /webhooks/** that reads DASHBOARD_API_URL per request and proxies with redirect: "manual" to keep OAuth 3xx hops intact, throwing if DASHBOARD_API_URL is unset so there is no production backend default.

During SSR the dashboard fetch layer copies the incoming request's cookie header onto forwarded requests because credentials: "include" is meaningless on the server, and it targets DASHBOARD_API_URL directly instead of a relative origin.

The experimental Electron desktop app ships the compiled web UI at an internal open-swe://app origin and proxies /dashboard/api/* to the user-configured backend so the browser never sees a LangSmith key or calls the raw LangGraph API, reusing the same signed dashboard session via a PKCE-bound desktop handoff exchanged at POST /auth/desktop/exchange.

Desktop "This Mac" local runs are supervised by Electron starting a loopback LangGraph server from langgraph.desktop.json, and agent/desktop.py gates them to an allowlisted local_project_path and builds a LocalShellBackend over that project, keeping the same graph/tools/streaming as cloud threads while differing only in filesystem backend and unavailable integrations.

Agent/UI parity is a product principle: anything users can do in the dashboard UI should generally also be possible through an agent tool subject to the same authorization and safety boundaries, and new dashboard endpoints are added in routes.py.
Authenticated users may read any thread whose metadata source is surfaced, while unsurfaced threads return 404; posting additionally requires admin for admin threads and automation threads.

Repository-scoped agent-instruction records are normalized by owner/repo, filtered and guarded by repository access in the API, and their non-empty text is appended to the main agent prompt for runs targeting that repository.

Review styles are repository-access-controlled records with an idle/running/completed/failed lifecycle; retrieval reconciles running analyses, concurrent analysis returns 409, and saved prompts allow a terminal or missing analysis run to resolve as completed.

Personal skills are isolated by GitHub login and represented as virtual SKILL.md records, while organization skills are shared, cursor-paginated, bounded in total count, readable by any session, and writable only by administrators.

Schedule listing requires authentication, but schedule creation, update, test triggering, and deletion require admin authorization; schedules are workspace-scoped records with cron and separate run state.

Schedule creation stores the record before creating a LangGraph cron but deletes the record and returns 502 if cron creation fails; enabled schedule changes create a replacement cron before the previous cron is removed, while disabling removes the cron.

Before a scheduled run, the system rechecks the schedule owner's repository access; on success it creates a new automation-classified thread and resumable durable agent run, and on loss of access it records an unauthorized run state instead of launching.

The thread listing API reserves all=true for administrators, supports a paginated filterable page view, and its sidebar separates active/resolved threads, excludes automation threads unless requested, and includes readable pinned threads.

Thread status normalization reports an interrupted latest run as interrupted even while the thread is temporarily busy, and marking a non-running thread viewed is fail-soft if the metadata update fails.

Focused dashboard thread tests cover model and image compatibility, lazy run-start metadata stamping, summary privacy behavior, terminal sandbox readiness, recovery patch limits, and the restriction that only run.start can create a missing thread.
